questions.question: What does Amazon EFS stand for?

options.text: Elastic Fragment Storage
Elastic File System
Encrypted File Store
Extensible File Server

explanation.correct: EFS stands for Elastic File System — a managed NFS-based file system that scales elastically.
explanation.why: A, C, and D are not real AWS services.

questions.question: Which protocol does Amazon EFS use for file system access?

options.text: SMB (Server Message Block)
iSCSI
NFSv4
FTP

explanation.correct: EFS uses the NFSv4 (Network File System version 4) protocol for all file system communication.
explanation.why: SMB is used by Windows file sharing (FSx for Windows); iSCSI is block storage; FTP is file transfer, not a file system protocol.

questions.question: What port must be open in security groups for an EC2 instance to mount an EFS file system?

options.text: Port 22
Port 443
Port 2049
Port 3306

explanation.correct: EFS uses port 2049 (the standard NFS port) for all communication. This must be allowed in the security group attached to the EFS mount target.
explanation.why: Port 22 is SSH; port 443 is HTTPS; port 3306 is MySQL/RDS.

questions.question: How many EC2 instances can mount an EFS file system simultaneously?

options.text: Thousands — no practical limit

explanation.correct: EFS supports thousands of concurrent NFS connections. There is no practical limit on the number of EC2 instances that can mount the same EFS file system simultaneously.
explanation.why: A is for EBS (one instance per volume); B and C are arbitrary limits that do not apply to EFS.

questions.question: What is a Mount Target in Amazon EFS?

options.text: An IAM role that grants EC2 access to EFS
An NFS endpoint in a specific VPC subnet/AZ that EC2 instances connect to
A DNS record that points to the EFS file system
A security group rule allowing NFS traffic

explanation.correct: A mount target is an NFS endpoint (with its own IP and DNS) created in a specific AZ subnet. EC2 instances connect to the mount target in their AZ to access EFS.
explanation.why: A describes IAM; C is not what a mount target is (though it has a DNS name); D is a security group rule, not a mount target.

questions.question: What is the key difference between EFS Standard and EFS One Zone storage classes?

options.text: Standard supports encryption; One Zone does not
Standard stores data across multiple AZs; One Zone stores in a single AZ
Standard is for Linux; One Zone is for Windows
Standard supports NFS; One Zone supports SMB

explanation.correct: EFS Standard replicates data across multiple AZs for high availability. EFS One Zone stores data in a single AZ — lower cost but data is at risk if that AZ fails.
explanation.why: A is wrong (both support encryption); C is wrong (both are Linux-only); D is wrong (both use NFS).

questions.question: Which operating systems are supported by Amazon EFS?

options.text: Windows only
Linux only
Linux and Windows
Any OS that supports block storage

explanation.correct: Amazon EFS is Linux-only due to its POSIX-compliance requirement. For Windows shared file storage, use Amazon FSx for Windows File Server.
explanation.why: A, C, and D are incorrect. EFS does not support Windows.

questions.question: What is the EFS General Purpose performance mode optimized for?

options.text: Highest aggregate throughput for massively parallel workloads
Lowest latency per file operation — default for most workloads
Lowest cost file storage
Single-AZ, fast access

explanation.correct: General Purpose is the default EFS performance mode, optimized for low latency per file operation. It is recommended for web servers, CMS, home directories, and most common workloads.
explanation.why: A describes Max I/O mode; C is about storage class pricing; D is about One Zone class.

questions.question: Can you change the performance mode of an EFS file system after it is created?

options.text: Yes — at any time via the console
Yes — only when no instances are connected
No — performance mode is set at creation and cannot be changed
Yes — using the modify-file-system AWS CLI command

explanation.correct: EFS performance mode (General Purpose or Max I/O) is set at file system creation time and cannot be changed afterward. You would need to create a new file system and migrate data.
explanation.why: A, B, and D are all incorrect — this is a permanent configuration choice.

questions.question: What is the pricing model for Amazon EFS?

options.text: Per hour per file system
Fixed monthly fee per GB provisioned
Per GB stored per month — you pay for actual usage, no provisioning needed
Per connection per month

explanation.correct: EFS charges per GB of data actually stored per month. There is no provisioning, no minimum fee, and no per-connection charge. You pay only for what you store.
explanation.why: A is incorrect; B is how EBS works (provisioned); D is incorrect.

questions.question: What does EFS lifecycle management do?

options.text: Automatically deletes files after a specified time
Automatically moves files to lower-cost IA storage classes based on last-access time
Compresses files to save storage space
Replicates files to another region automatically

explanation.correct: EFS lifecycle management automatically transitions files to Infrequent Access (IA) storage classes when they have not been accessed for a configured period (e.g., 30 days), saving up to 92% on storage costs for those files.
explanation.why: A is incorrect (files are moved, not deleted); C is not a feature; D is cross-region replication, a separate feature.

questions.question: What is the Max I/O performance mode designed for?

options.text: Single instance requiring fastest possible access
Massively parallel workloads with hundreds of instances requiring highest aggregate throughput
Database workloads requiring sub-millisecond latency
Archive workloads with rare access

explanation.correct: Max I/O is designed for workloads where hundreds of EC2 instances access the file system simultaneously and need the highest possible aggregate throughput. It has slightly higher per-operation latency than General Purpose.
explanation.why: A fits General Purpose better; C fits EBS with Provisioned IOPS; D fits IA storage classes.

questions.question: A company needs shared file storage for 50 Linux EC2 instances and 20 Windows EC2 instances. Which service(s) would you use?

options.text: EFS for all 70 instances
EBS for all 70 instances
EFS for the 50 Linux instances and FSx for Windows for the 20 Windows instances
S3 for all 70 instances

explanation.correct: EFS is Linux-only (POSIX NFS). For Windows instances needing shared file storage, Amazon FSx for Windows File Server is the correct choice. You would use both services in parallel.
explanation.why: A is wrong (EFS doesn't support Windows); B is wrong (EBS can't be shared); D is object storage, not a file system.

questions.question: An EFS file system is in Standard storage class. A lifecycle policy moves files to Standard-IA after 30 days of no access. A file in IA is then accessed — what happens?

options.text: The file stays in Standard-IA permanently
The file is automatically moved back to Standard storage class upon access
The file must be manually promoted back to Standard
The file is deleted from IA and a new copy is made in Standard

explanation.correct: When an IA-class file is accessed, EFS automatically moves it back to Standard storage for faster subsequent access. You pay a one-time retrieval fee for this transition.
explanation.why: A is incorrect; C and D are not how EFS works.

questions.question: Your EFS mount is failing. You can SSH to the EC2 instance and it is in the same VPC as the EFS mount target. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The EFS file system is in a different region
Port 2049 is not allowed in the EC2 or mount target security group
The EC2 instance type is not supported for NFS
EFS requires an Elastic IP for mounting

explanation.correct: The most common EFS mount failure is a missing security group rule for port 2049 (NFS). Check both the mount target's security group (inbound 2049 from EC2 SG) and the EC2 SG (outbound 2049).
explanation.why: A would cause a complete connection failure, not a mount failure; C is false; D is false.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the _netdev mount option in /etc/fstab for EFS?

options.text: It encrypts the EFS mount in transit
It tells Linux to wait for network availability before mounting — prevents boot failures
It sets the NFS version to version 4
It disables local caching for the EFS mount

explanation.correct: The _netdev option tells the Linux init system to defer this filesystem mount until the network is available. Without it, the mount may fail at boot because the network isn't up yet when /etc/fstab is processed.
explanation.why: A requires the tls option; C requires nfsvers=4.1; D is not what _netdev does.

questions.question: What is an EFS Access Point and why is it useful?

options.text: A VPN tunnel for securely connecting on-premises servers to EFS
An application-specific entry point that enforces a POSIX user identity and root directory for all connections
An AWS PrivateLink endpoint for EFS
A second mount target for failover in case the primary fails

explanation.correct: An EFS Access Point enforces a specific POSIX user (UID/GID) and a root directory for all connections through it. This allows multiple applications to share the same EFS file system with isolated access — each app sees only its subdirectory.
explanation.why: A is AWS Direct Connect or VPN; C is about PrivateLink, different feature; D is not a real EFS concept.

questions.question: How does EFS Bursting Throughput work?

options.text: You provision a fixed throughput amount and AWS guarantees it at all times
Throughput scales automatically based on demand with no configuration
The file system earns burst credits when idle and spends them during high-activity periods
Throughput is always capped at 50 MiB/s regardless of file system size

explanation.correct: Bursting Throughput works like EC2 T-class burstable instances — the file system earns burst credits when throughput is below the baseline and spends them during peaks. The baseline is 50 MiB/s per TiB of storage.
explanation.why: A describes Provisioned Throughput; B describes Elastic Throughput; D is not accurate.

questions.question: Which EFS throughput mode should you choose for a small file system (5GB) that requires consistently high throughput (500 MiB/s)?

options.text: Elastic Throughput
Bursting Throughput
Provisioned Throughput
Max I/O Throughput

explanation.correct: Provisioned Throughput lets you specify a fixed MiB/s independent of file system size. For a 5GB file system needing 500 MiB/s, the size-based allocation in Elastic or Bursting mode would be far too low. Provisioned Throughput solves this.
explanation.why: Elastic and Bursting both scale based on file system size; Max I/O is a performance mode, not a throughput mode.

questions.question: What is the correct order of steps to mount EFS on an EC2 Amazon Linux instance?

options.text: Create IAM role → Mount → Install NFS client → Configure security group
Install NFS client → Create mount directory → Mount with NFS command → Verify with df -h
Configure VPC endpoint → Install NFS client → Mount → Verify
Create S3 bucket → Install NFS client → Mount → Verify

explanation.correct: Correct order: (1) Install nfs-utils, (2) create a mount directory like /mnt/efs, (3) run the mount command using the EFS DNS name and NFSv4 options, (4) verify with df -h to confirm it appears in mount list.
explanation.why: A, C, and D have incorrect or unnecessary steps in wrong order.

questions.question: A media company needs a shared file system for video editing with 200 concurrent EC2 instances reading 4K source files (100GB each). Each instance needs maximum read throughput. Which EFS configuration is optimal?

options.text: General Purpose mode, Elastic Throughput, Standard storage class
Max I/O mode, Provisioned Throughput at required MiB/s, Standard storage class
General Purpose mode, Bursting Throughput, One Zone storage class
Max I/O mode, Elastic Throughput, Standard-IA storage class

explanation.correct: Max I/O mode handles hundreds of concurrent connections and maximizes aggregate throughput. Provisioned Throughput ensures consistent high MiB/s regardless of file system size. Standard storage class is correct for active files. Standard-IA would add retrieval latency for every read — wrong for active video editing.
explanation.why: A's General Purpose mode hits per-operation latency limits with 200 clients; C's Bursting and One Zone are wrong for production video; D's IA class adds latency for every file read.

questions.question: How does encryption at rest differ from encryption in transit in EFS, and how do you enable each?

options.text: They are the same feature — enabling one enables the other automatically
At rest: enabled at creation with KMS key; In transit: enabled via TLS mount flag (amazon-efs-utils or mount option tls)
At rest: enabled via CloudTrail; In transit: enabled via S3 bucket policy
At rest: enabled automatically; In transit: requires VPN connection

explanation.correct: These are two independent security features. Encryption at rest uses KMS (enabled at file system creation — cannot be enabled after). Encryption in transit uses TLS and is enabled at mount time using the amazon-efs-utils mount helper (mount -t efs -o tls) or the tls NFS mount option.
explanation.why: A is wrong — they are separate; C and D have incorrect mechanisms.

questions.question: You have an EFS file system where 90% of data is over 180 days old and never accessed, but 10% is actively used daily. Storage costs are very high. What is the most cost-effective solution?

options.text: Move the entire file system to One Zone storage class
Enable lifecycle management to transition files not accessed in 30 days to Standard-IA
Delete the EFS file system and use EBS instead
Enable compression on the EFS file system

explanation.correct: Enabling lifecycle management to move infrequently accessed files to Standard-IA (90% of files) can reduce storage costs by up to 92% for those files, while keeping the active 10% in Standard for fast access. This is exactly the use case lifecycle management was designed for.
explanation.why: A moves everything to single-AZ, risking the active 10%; C is wrong (you lose multi-instance sharing); D is not an EFS feature.

questions.question: What happens to an EFS One Zone file system if the Availability Zone it is hosted in experiences an outage?

options.text: EFS automatically fails over to another AZ within minutes
The file system remains available at reduced capacity
The file system becomes unavailable for the duration of the AZ outage, and data may be lost
EFS creates a read-only replica in another AZ automatically

explanation.correct: EFS One Zone stores data in a single AZ. If that AZ fails, the file system becomes completely unavailable for the duration of the outage. Unlike EFS Standard (which replicates across AZs), One Zone does not have cross-AZ redundancy.
explanation.why: A, B, and D describe behaviors of multi-AZ storage classes, not One Zone.

questions.question: A startup needs to run a containerized application on Amazon ECS (Fargate) where each task needs access to a shared configuration directory. Which EFS feature enables this and what is required?

options.text: EFS does not support ECS Fargate
EFS volume mounts in ECS task definitions — requires VPC, mount targets in the same VPC, and the efs:ClientMount IAM permission in the task role
Configure an S3 bucket as a volume mount — ECS Fargate requires S3 volumes
Use EBS Multi-Attach instead of EFS for ECS Fargate

explanation.correct: ECS Fargate natively supports EFS volumes. You specify the EFS file system ID in the task definition's volume configuration. The Fargate task must be in a VPC with mount targets in its subnets, and the task execution role needs efs:ClientMount permission (plus elasticfilesystem:ClientWrite if writing).
explanation.why: A is incorrect — Fargate has supported EFS since 2020; C is wrong (S3 is not a native volume mount); D is wrong (EBS Multi-Attach is for block storage, not recommended for ECS).

questions.question: Your EFS file system uses Bursting Throughput. After a year of low activity, the file system has accumulated maximum burst credits. A data migration suddenly writes 5TB continuously. What happens to throughput during the migration?

options.text: Throughput stays at base rate (50 MiB/s per TiB) throughout
Throughput bursts at maximum rate until burst credits are exhausted, then drops to baseline
Throughput is unlimited because burst credits have been fully accumulated
Throughput automatically switches to Provisioned mode during high usage

explanation.correct: During the migration, EFS spends the accumulated burst credits to sustain burst throughput. Once credits are exhausted, throughput drops to the baseline rate (50 MiB/s per TiB of storage). The migration completes at baseline speed from that point.
explanation.why: A ignores burst credits; C is wrong — burst credits have a maximum cap; D is not an automatic behavior.

questions.question: What is the correct EFS storage class for a disaster recovery copy of production data that is rarely accessed but must be available immediately when needed?

options.text: EFS One Zone-IA
EFS Standard-IA
EFS Standard
EFS One Zone

explanation.correct: EFS Standard-IA is correct — it replicates across multiple AZs (important for DR data that must survive AZ failures), costs ~93% less than Standard for storage, and makes files available immediately (with a per-request retrieval fee). One Zone classes risk data loss if the AZ fails, which defeats the DR purpose.
explanation.why: A and D use a single AZ — unacceptable for DR; C is too expensive for rarely-accessed data.

questions.question: An application team wants multiple microservices to share EFS but each service should only see its own directory and run as its designated user. Which feature enables this isolation?

options.text: Separate EFS file systems per microservice
EFS Access Points — one per microservice with enforced POSIX user and root directory
EFS Security Groups — one per microservice
VPC subnets — place each microservice in its own subnet

explanation.correct: EFS Access Points enforce a specific root directory and POSIX user identity (UID/GID) for all connections through that access point. Each microservice gets its own access point — it sees only its own directory even though all share the same underlying file system.
explanation.why: A is possible but costly and operationally complex; C and D are network-level isolation, not file-level isolation.

questions.question: Your team needs EFS to be accessible from on-premises servers. What connectivity option do you need?

options.text: An internet-facing EFS endpoint with public IP
AWS Direct Connect or AWS VPN to connect the on-premises network to the AWS VPC where EFS mount targets exist
EFS does not support on-premises access
Deploy an EC2 instance as an NFS proxy between on-premises and EFS

explanation.correct: EFS mount targets are private VPC resources. To access them from on-premises, you need private network connectivity via AWS Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN. Once connected, on-premises Linux servers can mount EFS using the same NFS commands as EC2 instances.
explanation.why: A is incorrect — EFS mount targets don't have public IPs by default; C is incorrect; D is a workaround but not the recommended AWS approach.

questions.question: What is the maximum single file size supported by Amazon EFS?

options.text: 5 TB
16 TB
47.9 TiB
Petabyte scale — no single-file limit

explanation.correct: Amazon EFS supports individual file sizes up to 47.9 TiB. The total file system can grow to petabyte scale, but individual files are bounded at 47.9 TiB per file.
explanation.why: 5 TB is the S3 single-object limit; 16 TB is an EBS maximum volume size; petabyte scale applies to the total file system, not individual files.
